name: No Timing
explanation: This is the strictest version of the timing criteria: timing can't be a required part of completing the activity at all, not even with a way to extend it. The narrow exceptions are non-interactive synchronized media, like a pre-recorded video with captions, where timing is fundamental to the content itself, and genuine real-time events, like a live auction, where a delay would defeat the purpose. Outside those two exceptions, if a user could still complete the task successfully given unlimited time, then no time limit should be imposed at all.
whoItAffects: People with cognitive disabilities, motor disabilities, or anyone who processes information more slowly, whether due to disability, unfamiliarity with the interface, or using assistive technology that takes more steps to complete an action, benefit from never facing a countdown at all. This goes further than SC 2.2.1's adjustable-timing accommodation: rather than requiring the user to notice a warning and act on it in time, this removes the pressure entirely, which matters most for tasks like completing a purchase, filling out a long form, or taking an assessment.
howToTest: Identify any task on the site that has a time limit of any kind, including ones that already meet SC 2.2.1 by offering extensions or warnings. For each one, ask whether the underlying activity is a genuine real-time event, like bidding in a live auction, or non-interactive synchronized media, like watching a captioned video. If it's neither of those, this AAA criterion requires removing the time limit altogether rather than just making it adjustable.

check.question: A job application form gives users 15 minutes to complete it, with a warning and the ability to request a 15-minute extension before time runs out — satisfying SC 2.2.1. Does this also satisfy the stricter SC 2.2.3 No Timing?
choices: Yes, because meeting SC 2.2.1 automatically satisfies SC 2.2.3
No, because SC 2.2.3 requires no time limit at all for a non-real-time, non-synchronized-media activity like this
Yes, because 15 minutes plus an extension is generous enough
It depends only on whether the extension can be requested more than once
